sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: CFA pile static capacity falls between drilled shafts and driven piles because installation leaves soil stresses near pre-construction values (DD piles raise them). Section 5.2 gives the general framework, 5.3 the recommended methods for conventional CFA piles, 5.4 a method for DD piles; computed resistances are estimates to be validated by load tests.
sections.body: In many respects the static capacity of a well-constructed CFA pile falls between that of a drilled shaft and a driven pile, mainly because of the different lateral stress changes during installation: stresses tend to reduce or stay unchanged around a drilled shaft, increase around a driven pile, stay near pre-construction values for conventional CFA piles (like a drilled shaft) and increase for drilled displacement (DD) piles (like driven piles). Methods developed for driven piles and drilled shafts are reasonable because the load-settlement behavior is similar; some methods developed for CFA piles modify them and correlate measured capacity with SPT blowcount, CPT tip resistance and undrained shear strength. The methods in Section 5.2 were chosen as generally reliable for conventional CFA piles according to four comparison studies (Appendix A summarizes these and other methods); Section 5.3 presents a method for DD piles, as printed. The chapter also covers group behavior, settlement and lateral capacity, used in Chapter 6's design procedure. Computed static axial resistances are estimates to be validated or modified by project load tests; the Chapter 8 performance-based specification makes the contractor responsible for computing resistance, setting pile lengths and verifying performance by load tests. (p. 64)

sections.title: Development of Side-Shear and End-Bearing Resistance with Pile Displacement
sections.summary: Total resistance is side-shear plus end-bearing (Eq. 5.1), side-shear summed over pile segments (Eqs. 5.2, 5.3) and end-bearing from unit base resistance (Eq. 5.4). Side-shear mobilizes at under about 10 mm (0.4 in.); end-bearing at 5% to 10% of the diameter; the methods define ultimate end-bearing at a tip displacement of 5% of the diameter (Figure 5.1). Elastic compression is usually small.
sections.body: The total axial compressive resistance R_T of a CFA pile is the side-shear resistance R_S plus the end-bearing resistance R_B (Eq. 5.1). The pile is divided into N segments; each segment's side resistance is its unit side-shear f_s,i (sometimes called load transfer rate) times its surface area pi D_i L_i, summed over all segments (Eq. 5.2); some methods use an average unit side-shear over the whole length (Eq. 5.3). R_B is the unit end-bearing q_p times the base area (Eq. 5.4). Side-shear is mobilized at relatively small displacements, typically under 10 mm (0.4 in.); end-bearing is fully mobilized at a tip movement typically 5% to 10% of the diameter. Driven piles mobilize tip resistance at smaller displacement owing to preloading during installation, so a CFA load test curve may look softer and driven-pile interpretation methods could be conservative for CFA piles (p. 65). Mobilized side and base resistances can be assessed with Figure 5.1 (Reese and O'Neill, 1988, for drilled shafts): resistance at a displacement ratio is the ultimate times the normalized resistance. Reese and O'Neill (1988), AASHTO (2006) and others take ultimate end-bearing at a tip displacement of 5% of the diameter, and the methods in this document use that definition unless noted. Elastic compression is relatively small for typical CFA lengths and loads and can often be disregarded: e.g., 445 kN (100 kip) on a 450 mm (18 in.), 25 m (82 ft) pile with E = 27,500 MPa (4,000 ksi), half the load to the tip and uniform side-shear, gives an average load of 0.75 of the load, 334 kN (75 kips), and shortening 334 kN x 25 m / (A_pile E) = 2 mm (0.08 in.); details in Section 5.5.3.1 (p. 66). (pp. 65 to 66)
key_points: R_T = R_S + R_B; side-shear summed over pile segments (Eqs. 5.1, 5.2) (p. 65).
Side-shear mobilized typically at less than 10 mm (0.4 in.) of displacement (p. 65).
End-bearing fully mobilized at a tip movement of 5% to 10% of the diameter (p. 65).

equations: Eq. 5.1: R_T = R_S + R_B; R_T = total axial compressive resistance, R_S = side-shear resistance, R_B = end-bearing resistance (p. 65)
Eq. 5.2: R_S = sum over i = 1 to N of f_s,i pi D_i L_i; f_s,i = unit side-shear resistance of segment i, D_i and L_i = its diameter and length, N = number of pile segments (p. 65)
Eq. 5.3: R_S = f_s-ave pi D L; f_s-ave = average unit side-shear over the pile length, D = average pile diameter, L = total embedment length (p. 65)
Eq. 5.4: R_B = q_p (pi D_B^2 / 4); q_p = unit end-bearing resistance, D_B = pile diameter at the base (p. 65)

sections.title: Recommended Methods for Estimating Static Axial Capacity of CFA Piles
sections.summary: The recommended methods assume conventional CFA construction with quality assurance that avoids excessive flighting and ground loosening; DD piles and amelioration are in Section 5.4. Methods are grouped by cohesive or cohesionless behavior (silty soils need judgment on drained or undrained response) and by the available test data; Figure 5.1 gives load-displacement curves. Load testing is a critical part of CFA pile use.
sections.body: The recommended methods for single CFA piles assume a conventional continuous flight auger technique with construction and quality assurance practices as recommended herein, so excessive flighting of soil and ground loosening are avoided. High-displacement (DD) piles or amelioration (coarse sand or gravel introduced from the surface into the annulus between borehole wall and drill stem) could significantly increase capacity (Section 5.4). Procedures are organized by soil type as cohesive or cohesionless; silty soils need the engineer's judgment, classifying fine-grained soils by whether they will behave more nearly undrained or fully drained under the load considered; recommendations are further grouped by the type of in-situ or laboratory data. Appendix A gives the comparison studies behind the choice and other methods (p. 66). Figure 5.1 (Reese and O'Neill, 1988) gives normalized side-shear and end-bearing vs. settlement (p. 67). The procedures correlate well for generalized soils across North American practice, but the engineer should consider the site's soil composition, construction techniques and local experience and may investigate alternative documented procedures matching the site; static estimates are useful for preliminary design, and a well designed load testing program is a critical and necessary component of effective CFA pile use (p. 68). (pp. 66 to 68)

sections.title: Recommended Method for Side-Shear and End-Bearing Estimates using Undrained Shear Strength
sections.summary: FHWA 1999 method (O'Neill and Reese, 1999) recommended for side-shear and end-bearing in cohesive soils: f_s = alpha Su, alpha = 0.55 for Su/Pa up to 1.5, then linear to 0.45 at 2.5; neglect the bottom one diameter and the top 1.5 m (5 ft) or seasonal moisture depth where shrinkage is possible. q_p = N*c Su with N*c = 9, or (4/3)(ln Ir + 1) (Table 5.1), reduced for L < 3D.
sections.body: The FHWA 1999 method for drilled shafts, proposed by Reese and O'Neill (1988) and modified by O'Neill and Reese (1999), is recommended for both side-shear and end-bearing of CFA piles in cohesive materials. Unit side-shear is f_s = alpha S_u (Eq. 5.5), with alpha = 0.55 for S_u/P_a <= 1.5 (Eq. 5.6), P_a being atmospheric pressure (about 101 kPa, 1.06 tsf), varying linearly from 0.55 to 0.45 for 1.5 < S_u/P_a <= 2.5. If the pile bottom bears on clay, side-shear of the bottom one-diameter length is neglected. If the top layer is clayey and may shrink away from the pile, its side-shear is neglected over the greater of the top 1.5 m (5 ft) or the depth of seasonal moisture change. Unit end-bearing is q_p = N*_c S_u (Eq. 5.7), S_u averaged from the tip to two diameters below; N*_c = 9 (Eq. 5.8) for 200 kPa (2 tsf) <= S_u <= 250 kPa (2.6 tsf) and L >= 3D (p. 68), or N*_c = (4/3)[ln I_r + 1] (Eq. 5.9) for S_u < 200 kPa (2 tsf) and L >= 3D, L being the embedment below top of grade. S_u above 250 kPa (2.6 tsf) is treated as intermediate geo-material per O'Neill and Reese (1999). The rigidity index I_r = E_s/(3 S_u) (Eq. 5.10) uses S_u and undrained Young's modulus just below the tip; E_s is best measured (triaxial or in-situ tests such as pressuremeter) or, with less accuracy, interpolated from Table 5.1. If the embedment were less than three diameters (not expected for CFA piles), q_p is reduced by Eq. 5.11 (p. 69). (pp. 68 to 69)

sections.title: Alternative Methods for Side-Shear Estimates using Undrained Shear Strength
sections.summary: Alternatives for side-shear from Su: Coleman and Arcement (2002), from Mississippi and Louisiana alluvial and loessial deposits, alpha = 56.2/Su (kPa) or 0.56/Su (tsf) for Su about 25 to 150 kPa (Figure 5.2), for very soft to medium deposits where FHWA 1999 may be too conservative; TXDOT 1971 for stiff desiccated clays, f_s = 0.7 Su up to 120 kPa (1.25 tsf).
sections.body: The Coleman and Arcement (2002) method was derived from CFA load tests in mixed soils, mostly alluvial and loessial deposits and interbedded sands and clays in Mississippi and Louisiana (Section A.2.10 of Appendix A), and may be considered for soils of similar geology; it modifies alpha for clays and silts behaving undrained (p. 69). Unit side-shear is f_s = alpha S_u (Eq. 5.12) with alpha = 56.2/S_u, S_u in kPa (Eq. 5.13a), or 0.56/S_u, S_u in tsf (Eq. 5.13b); coefficients are rounded, and the valid range of S_u is about 25 to 150 kPa (0.25 to 1.5 tsf) (Figure 5.2). In the FHWA 1999 method alpha would be 0.55 below about 150 kPa (1.5 tsf), reducing to 0.45; the engineer may use this correlation for similar deposits where FHWA 1999 may be too conservative for very soft to medium clays and silts (S_u up to about 50 kPa [0.5 tsf]). The TXDOT 1971 method (Texas Highway Department, 1972) for drilled shafts has given favorable results in stiff clays over-consolidated by desiccation: f_s = 0.7 S_u <= 120 kPa (1.25 tsf) (Eq. 5.14) (p. 70). (pp. 69 to 70)

sections.title: Alternative Method for Side-Shear and End-Bearing Estimates using SPT-N Values
sections.summary: Where only SPT-N values exist, Su may be estimated from local or published correlations, but this is recommended only for feasibility studies, not design, because SPT-N values are not highly reliable for undrained shear strength.
sections.body: Cohesive-soil methods rely almost exclusively on undrained shear strength. When only SPT-N values are available, S_u can be estimated with local or published correlations appropriate to the deposit, but this is recommended only in feasibility studies, not for design, because SPT-N values are not highly reliable for estimating undrained shear strength. (p. 71)

sections.title: Alternative Method for Side-Shear and End-Bearing Estimates using CPT Values
sections.summary: With CPT data, the LPC method (Bustamante and Gianeselli, 1981, 1982) is recommended over the other cohesive-soil methods: unit side-shear from Figure 5.3 by q_c, interpolating between the q_c < 1.2 MPa and q_c > 5 MPa curves; unit end-bearing q_p = 0.15 q_c, q_c averaged two to three diameters below the tip, whichever gives the lesser average.
sections.body: CPT testing has given good predictions of both end-bearing and side-shear of CFA piles and other deep foundations, is common in exploration and is preferred by many engineers; improved correlations may come as CPT use spreads. The LPC (Laboratoire des Ponts et Chaussees) method for drilled shafts and driven piles (Bustamante and Gianeselli, 1981, 1982) is recommended over the previous cohesive-soil methods when q_c data are available. Side-shear for undrained clays and silts comes from Figure 5.3: the unit side-shear (shown as maximum friction) at a depth is read from q_c there, interpolating between the limiting curves (q_c < 1.2 MPa [12.5 tsf] and q_c > 5 MPa [52 tsf]) by the average q_c along the pile or segment within the stratum. Unit end-bearing is q_p = 0.15 q_c (Eq. 5.16) (p. 71), with q_c averaged over two to three diameters below the tip, whichever gives the lesser average (p. 72). (pp. 71 to 72)

sections.title: Recommended Method for Side-Shear Estimates using Pile Depth and End-Bearing Estimates using SPT-N Values
sections.summary: FHWA 1999 method recommended in cohesionless soils, using N60 not depth corrected: f_s = K sigma'v tan phi = beta sigma'v <= 200 kPa (2.0 tsf), beta = 1.5 - 0.135 Z^0.5 (Z in ft) for N >= 15, scaled by N/15 below, limited to 0.25 to 1.2; q_p (tsf) = 0.6 N60 up to N60 = 75, 4.3 MPa (45 tsf) above.
sections.body: The FHWA 1999 method for drilled shafts (Reese and O'Neill, 1988; O'Neill and Reese, 1999) is recommended for CFA piles in cohesionless soils; it uses SPT N60 values (blows per 0.3 m or per foot [bpf]) at 60% hammer efficiency, not depth corrected. Unit side-shear is f_s = K sigma'_v tan phi <= 200 kPa (2.0 tsf) (Eq. 5.17) (p. 72), K being the lateral earth pressure coefficient, sigma'_v the vertical effective stress and phi the drained friction angle; beta = K tan phi (Eq. 5.18) is limited to 0.25 <= beta <= 1.2 and estimated as beta = 1.5 - 0.135 Z^0.5 for N >= 15 bpf (Eq. 5.19a) or (N/15)(1.5 - 0.135 Z^0.5) for N < 15 bpf (Eq. 5.19b), Z being the depth in feet to the middle of the layer or segment. Unit end-bearing is q_p (tsf) = 0.6 N60 for 0 <= N60 <= 75 (Eq. 5.20a) and 4.3 MPa [45 tsf] for N60 > 75 (Eq. 5.20b), N60 being near the tip, typically averaged from about one diameter above to 2 or 3 diameters below the tip (p. 73). sections.summary: Coleman and Arcement (2002) modify beta for drained sandy and silty soils of Mississippi and Louisiana: f_s = beta sigma_v <= 200 kPa (2.0 tsf), beta = 2.27 Zm^-0.67 (silty) or 10.72 Zm^-1.3 (sandy), Zm in meters, 0.2 to 2.5 (Figure 5.4). sections.body: The Coleman and Arcement (2002) method, from CFA load tests in Mississippi and Louisiana alluvial and loessial deposits and interbedded sands and clays (Section A.6.3 of Appendix A), modifies the FHWA 1999 beta for sandy and silty soils behaving drained: f_s = beta sigma_v <= 200 kPa (2.0 tsf) (Eq. 5.21), with beta = 2.27 Z_m^-0.67 for silty soils (Eq. 5.22) and beta = 10.72 Z_m^-1.3 for sandy soils (Eq. 5.23), Z_m being the depth in meters to the middle of the layer or segment, limited to 0.2 <= beta <= 2.5. sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: CFA piles have been used in strong non-caving materials (vuggy limestone, shale, weak rock), but penetration rates in hard material are too slow to prevent mining of caving overburden. With cohesive or stable overburden, follow drilled shaft procedures (O'Neill and Reese, 1999). Penetrate at least one diameter into rock; soil over extremely hard rock suits other foundations.
sections.body: CFA piles have been used successfully in strong, non-caving materials such as vuggy limestones, shales and other weathered or weak rocks, but it is generally not possible to install them in hard material at the penetration rate needed to cross caving soil without mining, so drilling a rock socket is comparable to an open-hole drilled shaft with the auger left in; the risk is mining of non-cohesive overburden while the socket is drilled. Where cohesive or stable overburden allows installation into weak or weathered rock without problems, computations should follow drilled shafts per O'Neill and Reese (1999). Over hard rock it may be difficult to get sufficient base resistance without mining; piles should penetrate at least one diameter into the rock to use its end-bearing (p. 75). Even with cohesive overburden, the pile/rock interface is uncertain unless rock penetration is assured; soil over extremely hard rock is better suited to drilled shafts, micropiles or driven steel piles (p. 76). (pp. 75 to 76)
key_points: Drilling into hard material is too slow to avoid mining caving overburden (p. 75).
With stable overburden, compute rock sockets as drilled shafts (O'Neill and Reese, 1999) (p. 75).
Penetrate at least one pile diameter into the rock to use its end-bearing (p. 75).
Soil over extremely hard rock better suits drilled shafts, micropiles or driven steel piles (p. 76).

sections.title: Vuggy Limestone
sections.summary: For South Florida vuggy limestone (Miami and Fort Thompson formations), Frizzi and Meyer (2000) correlate unit side-shear with SPT-N60 (Figure 5.7) from over 60 load tests; scale matters, and small plug and anchor tests overpredict (Figure 5.6). Side-shear vs. displacement is in Figure 5.8; no end-bearing method was proposed.
sections.body: For vuggy limestone of South Florida or similar formations, CFA piles may be designed by the Frizzi and Meyer (2000) relationships, derived from over 60 load tests in the Miami and Fort Thompson limestones (Broward and Miami-Dade Counties). Figure 5.6 shows unconfined compressive strength vs. ultimate unit side-shear: Gupton and Logan (1984) from drilled shafts, Kaderabek and Reynolds (1981) from anchor pullout tests on cores, Ramos et al. (1994) mainly from field grout plug tests; smaller anchor and plug tests mobilize higher side-shear than larger foundations at low rock strength, so scale effects matter and CFA design correlations should be based on full-scale piles. In the Frizzi and Meyer (2000) method, unit side-shear in either formation is correlated with SPT-N60 (Figure 5.7), N60 at 60% efficiency not depth corrected; the data were limited to ultimate unit side-shear not exceeding approximately 9 and 8 MPa (94 to 84 tsf) for the Miami and Fort Thompson formations, as printed (the proposed relationships in Figure 5.7 end near 9 and 8 tons/ft2), and the smaller plug test data of Ramos et al. (1986, as printed) again appear unconservative. Figure 5.8 gives side-shear development f/f_max vs. displacement W/D (%) compared with Reese and O'Neill (1988) and Semeraro (1982); no end-bearing method was proposed. Most piles mobilized very high load at very low displacement, then behaved like the deflection-hardening response for granular soil (p. 76). Figures 5.6 and 5.7 are on p. 77, Figure 5.8 on p. 78. (pp. 76 to 78)
key_points: Frizzi and Meyer (2000): over 60 load tests in Miami and Fort Thompson limestones (p. 76).
Small-scale anchor and plug tests overpredict side-shear; base CFA correlations on full-scale piles (p. 76).
Unit side-shear correlated with SPT-N60 (not depth corrected) in Figure 5.7 (p. 76).
Printed data limit: about 9 and 8 MPa (94 to 84 tsf); Figure 5.7's relationships end near 9 and 8 tons/ft2 (p. 76).
No end-bearing method was proposed by Frizzi and Meyer (2000) (p. 76).

sections.title: Clay-Shale
sections.summary: For sockets in North-Central Texas clay-shale (qu 100 to 3,000 kPa), Vipulanandan et al. give a hyperbolic load-displacement curve (Eq. 5.25), Q_ult/(qu pi D L) = -0.11 L/D + 0.96 (Eq. 5.26) and rho_50/D = 15.8/(qu/Patm) % (Eq. 5.27). Example: D = 1.5 ft, qu = 20 tsf, L = 4.5 ft gives Q_ult = 267 tons and 170 tons at 0.25 in.
sections.body: For CFA piles socketed into clay-shale of North-Central Texas or similar formations, socket capacity may be estimated by Vipulanandan et al. (2005, as printed; 2004 elsewhere), from eight load tests in clay-shale with q_u of 100 to 3,000 kPa (1 to 30 tsf) (from Texas Cone Penetrometer values), clay and sandy clay overburden allowing sockets without appreciable mining, diameters 450 to 600 mm (18 to 24 in.) and lengths 12 to 25 m (40 to 83 ft). Relative load Q/Q_ult vs. relative displacement rho/D (Figure 5.9) follows the hyperbola of Eq. 5.25 (p. 78). Q_ult correlates with q_u, circumference pi D and socket length L (Eq. 5.26, Figure 5.10) (p. 79), and rho_50/D with q_u normalized by atmospheric pressure (Eq. 5.27, Figure 5.11). Method: normalize q_u, get rho_50/D from Figure 5.11 or Eq. 5.27, Q_ult from Figure 5.10 or Eq. 5.26, then Q for a range of displacements (p. 80). Example: D = 1.5 ft, q_u = 20 tsf, L = 3D = 4.5 ft; q_u/P_atm = 20 gives rho_50/D = 0.79%; Q_u = 20 x 3.14 x 1.5 x 4.5 (-0.11 x 3 + 0.96) = 267 tons; at 0.25 in., Q = 267 x [0.25/18 / (0.0079 + 0.25/18)] = 0.64 x 267 = 170 tons (p. 81). (pp. 78 to 81)
key_points: Eight load tests in clay-shale, qu 100 to 3,000 kPa (1 to 30 tsf), 450 to 600 mm piles (p. 78).
Hyperbolic relative load vs. relative displacement, Eq. 5.25 (p. 78).
Example: Q_ult = 267 tons, 170 tons at 0.25 in. displacement (p. 81).
equations: Eq. 5.25: Q/Q_ult = (rho/D) / (rho_50/D + rho/D); Q = resistance at displacement rho, Q_ult = ultimate resistance at very large displacement, D = pile diameter, rho_50/D = displacement-to-diameter ratio at Q/Q_ult = 0.5 (p. 78)
Eq. 5.26: Q_ult / (q_u pi D L) = -0.11 (L/D) + 0.96; q_u = unconfined compressive strength of the clay-shale, L = socket length (p. 79)
Eq. 5.27: rho_50/D [in %] = 15.8 / (q_u / P_atm); P_atm = atmospheric pressure (any consistent units) (p. 80)

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: DD piles, mostly proprietary, displace spoils and soil laterally, densifying it and raising lateral stress; results depend on the displaced volume (high or partial displacement), the stress increase, interface roughness and effective diameter. Ko may fall by a third for drilled shafts and nearly double for driven piles; CPT resistance rose 20% to 50% after displacement piles in sand.
sections.body: Many techniques and tools, mostly from specialty contractors or equipment makers, increase capacity over conventional CFA piles; their performance depends on the displaced soil volume relative to pile volume, the permanent lateral stress increase or soil improvement at the interface, interface roughness and effective diameter, and different techniques suit different soils (densification in sands; roughness or diameter in cohesive soils where saturated soil is unlikely to densify). In DD piles the spoils and surrounding soil are displaced laterally or compacted into the borehole wall; the relative displaced volume makes a 'high displacement' or 'partial displacement' pile; with amelioration, sand or gravel introduced at the top may be compacted into the wall. Localized densification and higher effective lateral stresses result. Kulhawy (1984) showed Ko may decrease by as much as one third (toward Ka) for drilled shafts and nearly double (toward Kp) for high-displacement driven piles; Webb et al. (1994) found 20% to 50% higher CPT resistance after displacement piles in sands; Nataraja and Cook (1983) found the stress increase also depends on uniformity coefficient, OCR and initial effective stress. (p. 82)
key_points: DD performance depends on displaced volume, lateral stress increase, roughness and effective diameter (p. 82).
High vs. partial displacement is set by displaced soil volume relative to pile volume (p. 82).
Ko may fall by a third for drilled shafts and nearly double for driven piles (Kulhawy, 1984) (p. 82).
CPT resistance 20% to 50% higher after displacement piles in sands (Webb et al., 1994) (p. 82).

sections.title: Recommended Method Using SPT-N Values or CPT Data
sections.summary: NeSmith (2002), from 22 compression and six pullout tests at 19 U.S. sites (Table 5.2), is recommended for DD piles in cohesionless soils that densify: f_s = 0.01 q_c + Ws or 0.05 N + Ws (tsf), limited to 0.16 or 0.21 MPa; q_p = 0.4 q_c + WT or 0.19 N60 + WT as printed (1.9 N60 in tsf in the text). Capacity is very sensitive to technique and must be verified by load tests and monitoring.
sections.body: The recommended method for DD piles is based on NeSmith (2002). Caution is warranted: capacity is very sensitive to construction technique and tooling and relies on specialty contractors; improved resistances must be verified for the site, technique and equipment by full-scale load tests, with automated monitoring and recording for all test and production piles (p. 82). NeSmith studied 22 compression and six pullout tests at 19 U.S. sites: diameters 0.36 to 0.46 m (14 to 18 in.), mostly 0.41 m (16 in.); lengths 6 to 21 m (20 to 69 ft), average about 13 m (43 ft); soils mostly clean sands and fine gravels to silty and clayey sands (Table 5.2), the highest-fines site (Brown and Drew, 2000, Piedmont) being clayey silts to silty clays with around 50% passing the #200 sieve. Ultimate capacity was taken at 25.4 mm (1 in.) of tip movement or a displacement rate of 0.057 mm/kN (0.02 in./ton), whichever came first (the rate never governed), with Chin (1970) extrapolation where needed. Unit side-shear (Figure 5.12), for cohesionless materials densified by displaced spoils, is f_S = 0.01 q_c + W_S for q_c <= 200 tsf (20 MPa) (Eq. 5.28) or f_S (tsf) = 0.05 N + W_S for N <= 50 (Eq. 5.29) (p. 83), printed in SI as f_S (MPa) = 0.005 N + W_S: W_S = 0 and f_s <= 0.16 MPa (1.7 tsf) for uniform, rounded materials with up to 40% fines; W_S = 0.05 MPa (0.5 tsf) and f_s <= 0.21 MPa (2.2 tsf) for well-graded angular materials with up to 10% fines; interpolate between. These q_c-based values are more than twice the LPC values for conventional CFA piles (Figure 5.5). Unit end-bearing (Figure 5.13), from q_c or N60 between about 4D above and 4D below the tip, is q_p = 0.4 q_c + W_T < 19 MPa (200 tsf) (Eq. 5.30) or q_p (MPa or tsf) = 0.19 N60 + W_T for N60 <= 50 (Eq. 5.31, as printed): W_T = 0 for q_p <= 7.2 MPa (75 tsf) and uniform rounded materials up to 40% fines, W_T = 1.34 MPa (14 tsf) for q_p <= 8.62 MPa (89 tsf) and well-graded angular materials up to 10% fines; interpolate between. For comparison, SPT end-bearing for CFA piles ranged 0.6 to 1.7 N60 (tsf) and for DD piles 1.9 N60 to 1.9 N60 + 14 tsf, as printed; LPC gave 0.375 q_c for CFA piles and the DD method 0.4 q_c to 0.4 q_c + 14 tsf (p. 84). Figures 5.12 and 5.13 are on pp. 85 and 86. (pp. 82 to 86)
key_points: DD capacity is very sensitive to technique; verify by full-scale load tests and monitoring (p. 82).

Ultimate at 25.4 mm (1 in.) tip movement or 0.057 mm/kN (0.02 in./ton) rate (p. 83).

sections.title: Amelioration
sections.summary: Amelioration feeds coarse sand or gravel into the borehole top; reversed flights above a packer force it into the wall. Brown and Drew (2000) found about 25% more side-shear with sand (16% for a pile within a group) and about 50% with crushed stone; group and amelioration gains are not additive. It relies on specialty contractors and must be verified by load tests.
sections.body: In amelioration, coarse sand or gravel is introduced into the top of the borehole as the specialty tool advances; a section of reversed flights above the normal flights, with a packer (enlarged drill stem) between, catches the material falling down the annulus and forces it into the borehole wall. Besides densifying soil and raising effective stress, Brown and Drew (2000) showed it helps in silty clays to clayey silts where the interface friction angle would otherwise be smaller: amelioration with sand raised an individual pile's side-shear by about 25%, but only 16% for a single pile tested within a group at 3 diameters; crushed stone (maximum aggregate typically 10 mm [0.4 in.]) raised it about 50%. The free-draining material may speed pore pressure dissipation and increase the effective diameter. Group and amelioration effects combined were less than their sum. The technique relies on specialty contractors and is typically contractor-proposed; performance-based specifications (Chapter 8) may encourage it. Improved capacities must be verified with full-scale load tests and automated monitoring for all piles; shorter piles may then make group effects and settlement controlling, and effects on adjacent structures may limit its use. (p. 87)
key_points: Reversed flights above a packer force introduced sand or gravel into the borehole wall (p. 87).
Sand amelioration: about 25% more side-shear for an individual pile, 16% within a group (p. 87).
Crushed stone amelioration: about 50% more side-shear (p. 87).
Group and amelioration gains combined are less than their sum (p. 87).
Shorter piles may make group effects and settlement controlling (p. 87).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Group capacity is not necessarily the sum of single pile capacities, since zones of influence overlap (Figure 5.14); evaluations should consider block failure and the pile cap's contribution (pile raft), and group settlement may exceed a single pile prediction.
sections.body: The axial capacity of a pile group is not necessarily the sum of single pile capacities: zones of influence may intersect depending on spacing (Figure 5.14). Evaluations should also consider block failure (p. 87) and the possible bearing contribution of the pile cap (occasionally termed a pile raft), and settlement of a group may often exceed that predicted from a single pile analysis (p. 88). (pp. 87 to 88)
key_points: Group capacity is not necessarily the sum of single pile capacities (p. 87).
Check block failure and the pile cap's contribution (pile raft) (pp. 87 to 88).
Group settlement may exceed single pile predictions (p. 88).

sections.title: Group Efficiencies
sections.summary: Group efficiency is group resistance over the sum of single pile resistances (Eq. 5.32). Displacement piles (driven, and to a lesser extent DD) can exceed 1.0; excavated piles (drilled shafts, conventional CFA) give 1.0 or less, more so in cohesionless soils; soil mining can reduce lateral stress at installed piles.
sections.body: Group efficiency eta_g is the ultimate group resistance over the sum of individual pile resistances (Eq. 5.32). Displacement piles (driven, and to a lesser extent DD piles) tend to raise effective stress, so overlapping densified zones can give efficiency above 1.0; excavated piles (drilled shafts and conventional CFA piles) tend to lower effective stress or at best keep it at-rest (Ko), giving 1.0 or less. Stress changes are more pronounced in cohesionless soils, and poorly controlled construction with soil mining can reduce the lateral stress of previously installed piles. (p. 89)
key_points: Efficiency = group resistance / sum of single pile resistances (Eq. 5.32) (p. 89).
Displacement piles can give efficiency above 1.0; excavated piles 1.0 or less (p. 89).
Soil mining during drilling can reduce lateral stress at previously installed piles (p. 89).
equations: Eq. 5.32: eta_g = R_ug / (sum over i = 1 to n of R_u,i); R_ug = ultimate resistance of the group, R_u,i = ultimate resistance of single pile i, n = number of piles (p. 89)

sections.title: Conventional CFA Pile Groups
sections.summary: Conventional CFA groups may use drilled shaft efficiencies if built properly (mining makes them much lower). Cohesionless: AASHTO (2002) 10.8.3.9.3, eta = 0.65 at 2.5D to 1.0 at 6D (0.7 at 3D), likely conservative (Figures 5.15, 5.16, Table 5.3). Cohesive: AASHTO 10.8.3.9.2 block failure, eta = R_Block/sum <= 1 (Eqs. 5.33, 5.34). Weak underlying layers need block and settlement checks.
sections.body: Groups of conventional CFA piles may be designed with drilled shaft efficiencies, which may be conservative with proper construction verified by monitoring; if soil mining occurs, efficiency would be substantially less than for drilled shafts, particularly in cohesionless soils. Overlapping zones and cap bearing tend to make piles, cap and soil act as a block, so block failure should be checked; it generally controls only in soft cohesive soils or cohesionless soils over a weak cohesive layer, and closer spacing raises its potential (p. 89). Cohesionless soils: absent site data, follow AASHTO (2002) 10.8.3.9.3 for drilled shafts regardless of cap contact: eta = 0.65 at 2.5 diameters center-to-center, 1.0 at 6.0 or more, linear between; 3 diameters gives 0.7. These are most likely conservative where the cap firmly contacts the ground or the soil is not loosened; small-scale field tests suggest 1.0 or more at 3 to 4 diameters and 0.67 as a lower bound. Model studies (Garg, 1979; Liu et al., 1985; Senna et al., 1993; 125 to 330 mm diameters, 8 to 24 diameters long, dry or moist sands above the water table; clean sands below the water table may be lower): Garg's groups with the cap in contact were consistently more efficient (Figure 5.15); Liu et al. give side and base effects for a 3 by 3 group (Figure 5.16) (p. 90); Senna et al. found efficiencies of 1.0 to 1.1 at 3 diameters (Table 5.3) (p. 92). AASHTO may thus be significantly conservative in some cases; group effects may be evaluated in the test pile program with post-construction SPT or CPT in the group and tests of an interior pile, justifying an alternate approach project by project. Cohesive soils: follow AASHTO (2002) 10.8.3.9.2: efficiency from block failure regardless of cap contact, limited to 1.0 (Eq. 5.33); R_Block is side-shear on the block periphery (Figure 5.17) plus end-bearing on its footprint (Eq. 5.34, as printed) (p. 92), usually using the pile-to-soil angle delta over the whole periphery and q_p over a zone about 2 to 3 times Z deep. Pile in a strong layer over a weak layer: check whether eta below 1.0 is warranted as in 'Section 5.5.2.1.2' (as printed; no such heading is printed), with the block extending to the weak layer; settlement (5.5.3.3) may require penetration below the compressible layer (p. 93). (pp. 89 to 93)
key_points: If soil mining occurs, CFA group efficiency would be substantially less than for drilled shafts (p. 89).
Block failure generally controls only in soft cohesive soils or over a weak cohesive layer (p. 89).
Cohesionless: eta = 0.65 at 2.5D to 1.0 at 6D, linear; 0.7 at 3D (AASHTO 2002 10.8.3.9.3) (p. 90).
Small-scale tests suggest 1.0 or more at 3 to 4 diameters, 0.67 a lower bound (p. 90).
A test pile program may justify less severe group effects project by project (p. 92).
Cohesive: efficiency from block failure, limited to 1.0 (AASHTO 2002 10.8.3.9.2) (p. 92).
Block end-bearing uses a zone about 2 to 3 times Z deep (p. 93).
Weak underlying layer: check block failure and settlement; may need penetration below it (p. 93).

sections.title: Drilled Displacement Pile Groups
sections.summary: DD pile groups behave like driven pile groups when displacement is at least 15% of pile volume. Cohesionless: eta = 1.0 (AASHTO 1996 10.7.3.10.3), spacing about 3D or more. Cohesive: 1.0 if Su > 100 kPa (1 tsf) or cap in firm contact; otherwise 0.7 at 3D to 1.0 at 6D. Always check block failure and weak underlying layers (punching, settlement).
sections.body: DD pile group efficiencies are comparable to driven displacement pile groups, and even modest displacement can avoid the negative installation effects of drilled foundations; the following apply where positive displacement of at least 15% of the pile volume is achieved. Cohesionless soils: follow AASHTO (1996) 10.7.3.10.3 for driven piles: eta = 1.0 regardless of cap contact; driven and DD groups typically exceed 1.0, but 1.0 is used for conservatism; adequate spacing is about 3 diameters or more. If a weak formation underlies, check efficiency with the Section 5.5.2.1 equation, R_Block 'as described in Section 5.5.3' (as printed) and R_u,i per Section 5.4. Cohesive soils: Brown and Drew (2000) found DD piles in Piedmont clayey silts to silty clays behave between driven and conventional CFA piles; unit side-shear of the interior pile of a 5-pile group at 3 diameters was about 100% higher than an isolated pile, and 90% higher with sand amelioration (p. 94). For S_u above 100 kPa (1 tsf) or a cap in firm contact, take 1.0; for S_u below 100 kPa with the cap not in firm contact, interpolate from 0.7 at 3 diameters to 1.0 at 6 or more. Always check block failure. A strong layer over a weak layer that stops DD penetration at shallow 'refusal' needs a punching shear check by the block concept, and settlement may be significant (p. 95). (pp. 94 to 95)
key_points: Applies where positive displacement is at least 15% of the pile volume (p. 94).
Cohesionless: DD group efficiency 1.0 (AASHTO 1996 10.7.3.10.3); spacing about 3D or more (p. 94).
Interior pile of a 5-pile DD group: about 100% more unit side-shear than an isolated pile (p. 94).
Cohesive: 1.0 if Su > 100 kPa (1 tsf) or cap in firm contact (p. 95).
Otherwise 0.7 at 3D increasing linearly to 1.0 at 6D or more (p. 95).
Shallow refusal on a strong layer over a weak one: check punching shear and settlement (p. 95).

sections.title: Settlement of Pile Groups
sections.summary: Group settlement is likely many times single pile settlement because the group stresses a deeper zone (Figure 5.18); it combines elastic pile compression and soil compression (cohesionless) or consolidation (cohesive). Consider the timing of loads; the driven pile methods that follow are taken as representative of CFA and DD groups.
sections.body: Load development with displacement of single piles was discussed in Section 5.2 and Appendix A, but group settlement is likely many times greater than predicted for individual piles, especially with compressible soils near the tips, because the group mobilizes a much deeper zone (Figure 5.18). Group settlement combines elastic compression of the piles and settlement of surrounding soils: nearly instantaneous compression in purely cohesionless soils and time-dependent consolidation in purely cohesive soils; layered profiles may have both (p. 95). Designers should consider the magnitude and timing of loads: settlement under dead loads already in place may be complete before settlement-sensitive connections are made, so perhaps only loads after the girder bearing plates are set matter. The simplified methods that follow were formulated for driven pile groups and are considered generally representative of CFA and DD groups; the deeper zone is unlikely to be much affected by installation differences (p. 96). (pp. 95 to 96)

Group settlement = elastic pile compression + soil compression or consolidation (p. 95).

sections.title: Elastic Compression of the Pile
sections.summary: Pile elastic compression depends on load, stiffness and load transfer; a pile is rigid if S_R = (L/B)(E_soil/E_pile) <= 0.010. Otherwise sum segment compressions (Eq. 5.36), or use half of Q_max L/(A E) for uniform side-shear (Eq. 5.37) and the full value as an upper bound (Eq. 5.38). Group load per pile may be taken as total over number of piles.
sections.body: The elastic compression of the pile depends on the imposed load, pile stiffness and load transfer. With the stiffness ratio S_R = (L/B)(E_soil/E_pile) (Eq. 5.35) (p. 96), a pile may be considered rigid for S_R <= about 0.010, its shortening very small compared with soil settlement; otherwise compression Delta should be estimated, included in settlement and subtracted from total displacement when assessing mobilized side and base stresses below ultimate. Delta is the sum over segments of Q_i L_i/(A_i E_i) (Eq. 5.36), the load falling from the total pile load at the top to the mobilized end-bearing at the tip (downdrag or uplift per Section 5.7). For a pile cap contributing as a raft with eccentric loads the load per pile is complex, but total group load divided by the number of piles may suffice. Uniform side-shear carrying all the load gives a triangular load distribution and Delta = (1/2) Q_max L_pile/(A_pile E_pile) (Eq. 5.37); a free-standing column with all load in end-bearing gives the upper bound Delta_max (Eq. 5.38) (p. 97), downdrag or swell aside (Section 5.7). Eqs. 5.37 and 5.38 give a quick estimate to judge whether a fuller load distribution analysis is justified (p. 98). (pp. 96 to 98)
key_points: Pile considered rigid if S_R = (L/B)(E_soil/E_pile) <= about 0.010 (p. 97).
Subtract elastic compression from total displacement when assessing mobilized stresses (p. 97).
Load per pile may be taken as total group load / number of piles (p. 97).
Uniform side-shear: Delta = (1/2) Q_max L / (A E); end-bearing only: upper bound Q_max L / (A E) (pp. 97 to 98).
equations: Eq. 5.35: S_R = (L/B)(E_soil/E_pile); L = embedment depth, B = pile diameter, E_soil = average soil Young's modulus, E_pile = pile Young's modulus; rigid if S_R <= about 0.010 (p. 96)
Eq. 5.36: Delta = sum over i = 1 to n of Q_i L_i / (A_i E_i); Q_i = average axial load in segment i, L_i, A_i, E_i = its length, average area and average composite modulus (p. 97)
Eq. 5.37: Delta = (1/2) Q_max L_pile / (A_pile E_pile); uniform unit side-shear with all load in side friction (triangular load distribution); Q_max = total maximum imposed load (p. 97)
Eq. 5.38: Delta_max = Q_max L_pile / (A_pile E_pile); upper bound, free-standing column with all load in end-bearing (p. 98)

The method does not specify 60% efficiency for N, but the 60% correction is recommended. sections.title: Consolidation Settlement in Cohesive Soils
sections.summary: Consolidation settlement of cohesive soils under sustained load uses the Terzaghi and Peck (1967) equivalent footing at D/3 above the toe, plan area B x Z, spreading at 1H:2V (Figures 5.19, 5.20), and layer settlements from e-log p curves (Figure 5.21) for overconsolidated (Eqs. 5.42, 5.43) and normally consolidated (Eq. 5.44) soil. Underconsolidated soil adds downdrag (5.7).
sections.body: Consolidation settlement of cohesive soils accompanies sustained loads as excess pore pressure dissipates; time rate is not addressed here (see geotechnical texts and FHWA NHI-06-088). Designing for the full sustained dead load is conservative; part of the dead load may already be in place before settlement-sensitive parts are built, so if total settlement matters, time rate under construction loads may be evaluated. A simplified stress distribution is usually sufficient: in the equivalent footing method (Terzaghi and Peck, 1967), the footing is placed 1/3 of the embedment D above the toe with the group plan area B x Z, and the load spreads within a frustum at 1 (horizontal) : 2 (vertical) (Figure 5.19); its depth may be adjusted for stratigraphy and load transfer (Figure 5.20). Soils below are divided into layers and settlements summed from laboratory e-log p curves (p. 99), with terms illustrated in Figure 5.21: for an overconsolidated layer with p_o + Delta p > p_c, Eq. 5.42; with p_o + Delta p < p_c, Eq. 5.43 (p. 100); for a normally consolidated layer (p_o = p_c), Eq. 5.44; Eqs. 5.42 and 5.43 print subscript sigma where the definitions list e_o and p_o. Underconsolidated soil (p_o > p_c) would keep consolidating and add downdrag to the group (Section 5.7) (p. 102). (pp. 99 to 102)
key_points: Designing for full sustained dead load is conservative (p. 99).
Equivalent footing at 1/3 of embedment D above the toe, plan area B x Z, spread 1H:2V (p. 99).
Adjust the equivalent footing depth for stratigraphy and load transfer (Figure 5.20) (p. 99).

Underconsolidated soil (po > pc) adds downdrag to the group (p. 102).

Eq. 5.44: S_i = H [C_c/(1 + e_o) log((p_o + Delta p)/p_o)]; normally consolidated layer (p_o = p_c) (p. 102)

sections.title: Uplift of Single CFA Piles and CFA Pile Groups
sections.summary: CFA piles behave as drilled shafts in uplift and are efficient (slender shape; a full-length high-strength bar). Uplift side-shear equals downward side-shear in cohesive soils and 0.8 of it in cohesionless soils; group uplift (AASHTO 1996) is the least of single allowable x n, 2/3 block weight, or 1/2 block weight plus 1/2 peripheral shear. Swelling soil uplift is a load with no reduction.
sections.body: CFA piles behave essentially as drilled shafts in uplift and can be particularly efficient because their long, slender shape maximizes side-shear per volume; placing enough steel may limit uplift, but a single high-strength bar can usually be placed full length. Uplift arises from external forces (resisted) or from swelling soils (a load). Ultimate upward side-shear is taken from the downward methods with opposite sign: the same magnitude in cohesive soils; in cohesionless soils studies show 70% to 100% of the downward value, and a factor of 0.8 on compressive side-shear is recommended, with safety factors still applied. Group uplift per AASHTO (1996) service load design is the least of (1) the single pile allowable uplift times the number of piles (allowable = one third of ultimate from static analysis, one half from a load test); (2) two thirds of the effective weight of the group and soil within the block (Figure 5.17); (3) one half of that weight plus one half of the soil shear on the block periphery. Swelling of expansive soils or ice jacking (frost heave, ice sheets) loads the pile (p. 103) by the ultimate downward side-shear with opposite sign, without the cohesionless reduction, since effective stress would not be reduced (p. 104). (pp. 103 to 104)
key_points: CFA piles behave as drilled shafts in uplift; a single high-strength bar can usually go full length (p. 103).
Cohesive: uplift side-shear equal to downward side-shear (p. 103).

Group uplift: least of n x single allowable, 2/3 block weight, 1/2 weight + 1/2 peripheral shear (p. 103).
Swelling soil uplift is a load; no cohesionless reduction applies (p. 104).

sections.title: Behavior and Limitations of CFA Piles
sections.summary: Lateral load tests show CFA piles behave like drilled shafts once material differences are accounted for, but limited reinforcement (cage to the high-moment zone, single full-length center bar), cage insertion into fresh grout (easier in cohesive soils, harder in draining sands) and diameters of 0.35 to 0.60 m limit lateral resistance. Batter piles and walls are possible.
sections.body: Though published results are limited, lateral load tests show CFA piles behave essentially like drilled shafts once material differences (grout or concrete, amount of steel) are accounted for (O'Neill et al., 2000, Texas over-consolidated clays; Frizzi and Meyer, 2000, Pamlico sand and Miami limestone). Because of reinforcement limits CFA piles generally provide less lateral resistance than drilled shafts and driven pile groups: a cage is usually set only through the high-moment zone, often with a single full-length center bar; structural H or pipe sections can be used as in micropiles. Cages are set into fresh grout (except some screw piles placed through the hollow auger), which limits full-depth penetration depending on soils and mix: in cohesive soils full cages often reach 45 m (150 ft) or more as water is retained; in free-draining sands, especially dry, bleed water loss limits workability and penetration. Diameters are typically 0.35 to 0.60 m (14 to 24 in.), rarely over 0.9 m (36 in.), leaving little room for a cage after cover. Batter piles can enhance group lateral stiffness, analyzed with GROUP (Ensoft, 2006) or FB-Pier (BSI, 2003) (p. 104), but are limited by settlement-induced ground movement and cage placement difficulty, and are not typical over water. Secant or tangent walls are analyzed like other deep foundations, with CFA size and depth limits and reinforcement installed after grouting (p. 105). (pp. 104 to 105)

Cages usually only through the high-moment zone, often with a single full-length center bar (p. 104).

sections.title: Lateral Analyses Using the p-y Method
sections.summary: The p-y method is recommended for laterally loaded CFA piles: a beam-column on nonlinear springs (Figure 5.22) governed by Eq. 5.45, with shear, moment and slope from Eqs. 5.46 to 5.48, iterated with secant moduli (Eq. 5.49). Head conditions: free head (force and moment) or fixed head (zero slope). Nonlinear steel and concrete models (Eqs. 5.50 to 5.54) give cracked-section EI (Figure 5.26).
sections.body: The p-y method is recommended for vertical CFA piles and groups; it handles combined axial and lateral loads, distributed loads, nonlinear bending (cracked sections), layered soil or rock and nonlinear soil response numerically. The pile is a beam with head loads and the soil a series of nonlinear springs (Figure 5.22); the soil reaction p per unit length at depth x is a nonlinear function of deflection y, depending on soil strength and stiffness, water level, diameter, depth and static or cyclic loading. Real p-y curves are curvilinear, correlated from instrumented full-scale tests; programs contain these models and accept user curves. Inputs: for cohesive soils S_u, epsilon_50 and unit weight; for cohesionless soils phi, subgrade modulus k and unit weight; and groundwater (p. 105). See Reese (1986) and O'Neill and Reese (1999). Loss of resistance from scour or liquefaction must be considered, and liquefaction over much of the length could be problematic for small CFA piles. The governing equation (Hetenyi, 1946) is Eq. 5.45 (p. 106); programs discretize pile and soil, giving p, shear V, moment M, slope S and deflection y at each node, with V, M and S from Eqs. 5.46 to 5.48 (FHWA-RD-85-106). Head conditions are lateral force P_t and moment M_t (free head, e.g., a cantilevered soundwall, sign or pole) or displacement, slope or rotational restraint; groups in a rigid cap with full moment connection approach fixed head (force plus zero slope) (p. 107). Figure 5.23 shows a restrained-head solution with maximum moment at the head. Each node uses a secant modulus E_s = p/y (Eq. 5.49), updated iteratively, which is stable and allows strain softening and cyclic degradation; steel and concrete stress-strain models are in Figures 5.24 and 5.25 (p. 108). Grade 60 steel has yield 413 MPa (60 ksi) and modulus 200,000 MPa (2,900 ksi), as printed, yield strain f_y/E (p. 109). Concrete follows Eqs. 5.50a and 5.50b with f''_c = 0.85 f'_c (Eq. 5.51) and epsilon_o = 1.7 f'_c/E_c (Eq. 5.52); E_c from Eq. 5.53 and tensile strength f_r from Eq. 5.54; the authors find the computed modulus somewhat conservative, and sand-cement grout may be slightly softer. EI drops at cracking; a concentric axial load gives a uniform compressive stress ('P_x x Area', as printed) that raises the cracking moment; programs include this (Figure 5.26) (p. 110). (pp. 105 to 111)

Cohesive input: Su, epsilon_50, unit weight; cohesionless: phi, subgrade modulus k, unit weight (p. 105).

Steel printed as 413 MPa (60 ksi) yield and 200,000 MPa (2,900 ksi) modulus (p. 109).

sections.title: Lateral Analyses of CFA Pile Groups
sections.summary: Group effects use p-multipliers (Pm < 1) by row (front, second, third and subsequent; Figure 5.27, Table 5.4), depending on position and spacing. A single average Pm gives group deflection and stiffness within about 20% for individual piles; increase computed maximum moment by 20% for design. Group lateral resistance is the sum of individual piles.
sections.body: The p-multiplier method is recommended for lateral group effects: p values of closely spaced piles are multiplied by P_m < 1 (Figure 5.27), so group capacity at a deflection is less than the sum of single piles and deflection at a load per pile is larger. P_m depends on position and spacing: front row piles are least affected, second rows more, third and subsequent rows most (the 'shadowing' effect). Table 5.4 gives values for cyclic and static loading (p. 111). GROUP (Ensoft, 2006) or FB-Pier (BSI, 2003) analyze the whole group. Brown and O'Neill (2003) suggest a simplified approach, useful when load direction is unknown: a single P_m equal to the average of all row values gives reasonably accurate group deflection and stiffness, individual pile shear and maximum moment deviating by no more than 20% typically; a single pile analysis then represents a typical group pile, with a 20% increase in computed maximum moment recommended for design. With LPILE (Ensoft, 2006) and P_m applied, a full moment connection gives a pile head with zero slope; group lateral resistance is the sum of individual piles (p. 113). (pp. 111 to 113)

sections.title: Structural Capacity
sections.summary: CFA structural capacity is checked like drilled shafts for axial load (including uplift), bending and shear from lateral analyses. Geotechnical design here is ASD, structural design LRFD per AASHTO (2006), so lateral analyses must include factored load cases.
sections.body: The structural capacity of CFA piles should be checked as for drilled shafts. Unlike typical non-redundant single shafts under columns, CFA piles are usually in groups with small per-pile bending, though single CFA piles under soundwalls, signs or light poles are dominated by flexure. Check axial loading (including uplift), bending and shear from lateral loading. Geotechnical design of CFA piles here follows allowable stress design (ASD); structural design follows LRFD per AASHTO (2006), so lateral analyses for structural moments must include factored load cases. (p. 113)

sections.title: Longitudinal Reinforcement
sections.summary: A top cage (multiple bars with spirals or ties) to the second zero of the deflection profile plus a single full-length center bar; the tapered bottom 1.2 m (4 ft) does not count. Minimum steel 1% of Ag (reduced effective area not below Ag/2). Design as short columns with an interaction diagram: P_n = beta P_S (Eq. 5.55), transition P' = 0.133 f'c Ag (Eq. 5.56), phi = 0.75 above P', 0.9 in pure flexure.
sections.body: CFA reinforcement typically has a top full cage of longitudinal bars with spirals or ties and a single full-length center bar. A center bar of virtually any size usually reaches full depth and suits uplift; high-strength threaded rods may be used as in micropiles. The full cage should extend to the inflexion point of the displacement profile (second point of zero displacement), e.g., about 7.5 m (25 ft) for the pile of Figure 5.23, so a full-length cage is unnecessary for a 15 or 18 m (50 or 60 ft) pile; short piles whose deflection does not cross zero twice need a full-length cage. Transverse steel is often omitted in about the bottom 1.2 m (4 ft), the bars bent inward to the center bar; this tapered section does not count toward the required cage length. Within the cage, longitudinal steel should be at least 1% of the gross area A_g, or of a reduced effective area A_g' (O'Neill and Reese, 1999; ACI 10.8.4) not less than A_g/2 where the pile is structurally oversized. A center bar must extend through the top cage and may be counted (p. 114). Design follows short columns: strain compatibility at ultimate (Figure 5.28, epsilon_c = 0.003), bars beyond yield at the yield stress, giving an interaction diagram (p. 115); all axial-moment combinations must lie within the factored diagram (Figure 5.29), obtainable from lateral analysis programs. Axial capacity is P_n = beta P_S (Eq. 5.55) (p. 116), beta = 0.85 for spirals and 0.80 for ties; the transition is P' (Eq. 5.56); above it the factored diagram is phi P_x and phi M_x with phi = 0.75 for spiral or tied reinforcement (Eq. 5.57, AASHTO 2006); pure flexure is 0.9 M, phi interpolated from 0.9 at P_x = 0 to 0.75 at P'. Bending usually controls CFA piles with large moments, near P_x = 0 (p. 117). (pp. 114 to 117)

sections.title: Shear Reinforcement
sections.summary: Check concrete shear first: phi Vn = phi Vc Av (Eq. 5.58, phi usually 0.85) with Av = B[B/2 + 0.58 r_ls] and Vc from Eqs. 5.61a/b. If short, enlarge the pile or design shear steel (Eq. 5.63). Minimum spiral ratio from Eq. 5.62; ties #3 (bars under #11) or #4, spaced at most the diameter or 300 mm (12 in.).
sections.body: First check whether the concrete section has adequate shear capacity: phi V_n = phi V_c A_V (Eq. 5.58), phi usually 0.85 (p. 117), with the effective area A_V = B[B/2 + 0.58 r_ls] (Eq. 5.59) and r_ls = B/2 - d_c - d_b/2 (Eq. 5.60). V_c is from Eq. 5.61a (psi) or 5.61b (MPa), reducing for P_x = 0 to V_C = sqrt(f'_c) (psi) or 0.166 sqrt(f'_c) (MPa), as printed. If factored shear resistance exceeds factored shear load, minimum transverse steel suffices; otherwise enlarge the pile or analyze shear steel, unusual for CFA piles since moments usually govern diameter. Minimum spiral ratio follows AASHTO (Eq. 5.62) (p. 118). Ties: #3 for longitudinal bars smaller than #11, #4 for #11 or larger, vertical spacing not more than the pile diameter or 300 mm (12 in.). If minimum transverse steel is inadequate: larger diameter, higher strength or more transverse steel, from Eq. 5.63 (p. 119). (pp. 117 to 119)
key_points: Factored concrete shear resistance phi Vc Av with phi usually 0.85 (p. 117).
For Px = 0, Vc = sqrt(f'c) (psi) or 0.166 sqrt(f'c) (MPa), as printed (p. 118).
Shear steel design is unusual for CFA piles; moments usually govern the diameter (p. 118).
Ties: #3 for bars smaller than #11, #4 for #11 or larger (p. 119).
Tie spacing not more than the pile diameter or 300 mm (12 in.) (p. 119).
equations: Eq. 5.58: phi V_n = phi V_c A_V; V_n = nominal shear resistance, phi = shear capacity reduction factor (usually 0.85), A_V = area effective in shear, V_c = concrete shear strength (p. 117)
Eq. 5.59: A_V = B [B/2 + 0.58 r_ls]; B = pile diameter (p. 118)
Eq. 5.60: r_ls = B/2 - d_c - d_b/2; r_ls = radius of the ring through the longitudinal bar centroids, d_c = cover depth, d_b = longitudinal bar diameter (p. 118)
Eq. 5.61a: V_C = (1 + 0.00019 phi P/A_g) sqrt(f'_c) (f'_c in psi); P = axial load, A_g = gross concrete area (p. 118)
Eq. 5.62: rho_S = 0.45 (A_g/A_c - 1)(f'_c/f_y); rho_S = volume of spiral steel per turn / volume of concrete core per turn, A_c = area inside the spiral, f_y = spiral yield strength (p. 118)

Eq. 5.63: A_vs = S V_steel / (f_y [B/2 + 0.58 r_ls]); A_vs = required transverse steel area, S = tie spacing (spiral pitch), V_steel = nominal shear resistance needed from the transverse steel (p. 119)

sections.title: Concrete or Grout Cover and Cage Centering Devices
sections.summary: AASHTO (2006) 5.12.3 cover applies: for W/C 0.40 to 0.50, 75 mm (3 in.) over longitudinal bars, 100 mm (4 in.) in aggressive environments; times 1.2 for W/C 0.50 or more, 0.8 for 0.40 or less. Centering devices are required: plastic wheels on full cages, skids on the center bar, oriented to roll or slide without scraping.
sections.body: The cover requirements of AASHTO (2006) Section 5.12.3 apply. For W/C between 0.40 and 0.50, minimum cover over longitudinal bars is 75 mm (3 in.), and 100 mm (4 in.) in aggressive environments (e.g., salt water); transverse steel cover may be less by no more than 12 mm (0.5 in.), so transverse bars over 13 mm (0.5 in.) would need more cover, which is rare for CFA piles. For W/C of 0.50 or more covers increase by 1.2; for 0.40 or less they may decrease by 0.8, though low W/C can hinder reinforcement placement. Centering devices must be used: for full cages, as for drilled shafts, most often plastic 'wheels' on the transverse steel; the center bar uses axisymmetric skids; wheels must roll and skids slide along the borehole wall without scraping soil. (p. 120)
key_points: Cover 75 mm (3 in.) over longitudinal bars; 100 mm (4 in.) in aggressive environments (p. 120).
Cover x 1.2 for W/C >= 0.50; x 0.8 allowed for W/C <= 0.40 (p. 120).
Centering devices required: plastic wheels on cages, skids on the center bar (p. 120).

sections.title: Seismic Considerations
sections.summary: For simple equivalent static seismic loads, design as in 5.6.2 and 5.6.3, with a full-length center bar for uplift. Liquefaction and lateral spreading can bend piles at great depth, needing deep reinforcement; a single center bar is not sufficient, and a continuous steel pipe may be considered.
sections.body: A full treatment of seismic design is beyond the manual's scope. For many transportation structures seismic design is an equivalent static analysis of inertial lateral loads at the foundation top, handled as in Sections 5.6.2 and 5.6.3; seismic uplift may require a full-length center bar (5.6.4.1). With soft ground, seismically induced ground movements, most significantly liquefaction and lateral spreading, can produce large bending stresses at great depth, so reinforcement may be needed deep to keep axial capacity during and after the event (p. 120); a single center bar is not sufficient, and a continuous steel pipe can give good flexural capacity and ductility where deep cages are problematic (p. 121). (pp. 120 to 121)
key_points: Equivalent static seismic loads: analyze as in 5.6.2 and 5.6.3 (p. 120).
Seismic uplift may require a full-length center bar (p. 120).
Liquefaction and lateral spreading may need deep reinforcement; a single center bar is not sufficient (pp. 120 to 121).
A continuous steel pipe may be considered where deep cages are problematic (p. 121).

sections.title: Downdrag in CFA Piles
sections.summary: Downdrag develops at 2.5 to 13 mm (0.1 to 0.5 in.) of relative movement and is treated as for drilled shafts, as a permanent load above the neutral plane (Figures 5.30 to 5.33). The neutral plane may be put conservatively at the top of a strong lower layer or found iteratively. Groups use an equivalent pier with modulus E_e (Eq. 5.64); at 3D spacing only perimeter piles get downdrag.
sections.body: CFA piles take downdrag (shear stress reversal) when soils around the upper pile move down relative to it; it develops fully at about 2.5 to 13 mm (0.1 to 0.5 in.), and analysis follows drilled shafts with the recommended side-shear methods, though CFA piles are always used in groups and group behavior may control. Cases (Figure 5.30): overlying loose sand, especially submerged in seismic areas, where liquefaction with limited deep flexural capacity may preclude CFA piles; overlying soft clay, a problem if surface load is added or excess pore pressures remain after installation; recently placed fill, such as abutment fill around the piles. Figure 5.31 shows the limit states: the left (applied plus downdrag load fails side and base in the founding stratum) is customarily the strength limit state for sustained loads, as the right (pile moving down more than the soil) needs settlements of several inches to several feet. Settlement (service) may control, and downdrag can add significantly to structural axial forces (p. 121). Downdrag is a permanent load from negative side-shear above the neutral plane (zero relative movement); resistance is the positive side-shear and end-bearing below it. The neutral point may be assumed, conservatively, at the top of a strong lower layer beneath a weak layer causing downdrag (Figure 5.32c, d; O'Neill and Reese, 1999), or found iteratively where end-bearing R_Bd matches static analysis or load tests (Figure 5.32e, f) (p. 122). For groups, an equivalent pier of the piles' depth and the group perimeter (Figure 5.33) with modulus E_e (Eq. 5.64) is used; at the typical 3-diameter spacing downdrag acts only around the group perimeter, not on interior piles (p. 123). Figures 5.32 and 5.33 are on p. 124. (pp. 121 to 124)
key_points: Downdrag fully develops at about 2.5 to 13 mm (0.1 to 0.5 in.) of relative movement (p. 121).
Loose submerged sand in seismic areas may preclude CFA piles (p. 121).
Left-side limit state of Figure 5.31 is the customary strength limit state for sustained loads (p. 121).
Downdrag is a permanent load above the neutral plane (p. 122).
Neutral point conservatively at the top of the strong lower layer, or found iteratively (p. 122).
Groups: equivalent pier with modulus Ee (Eq. 5.64) (p. 123).
At 3-diameter spacing downdrag acts only on the group perimeter, not interior piles (p. 123).
equations: Eq. 5.64: E_e = E_c (A_piles/A_group) + E_st (1 - A_piles/A_group); E_e = average modulus of the equivalent pier in the compressible layer, E_c = pile (concrete or grout) modulus, E_st = modulus of the geomaterial between piles, A_piles = area of all piles, A_group = group area excluding overhanging cap (p. 123)

sections.body: Side-shear at 60 ft by Section 5.3.1.1 (spreadsheet for a range of depths in Appendix B): the top layer (medium gray clay, CH) loses its top 5 ft (more if the cap bottom or seasonal moisture depth exceeded 5 ft) and the bottom layer (stiff to very stiff tan clay, CL to CH) its bottom diameter (1.5 ft). By Eq. 5.2 with D = 1.5 ft, L_top = 29 - 5 = 24 ft and L_bottom = 60 - 1.5 - 29 = 29.5 ft (p. 125). S_u,max = 2.5 ksf gives S_u,max/P_a about 1.25, so alpha = 0.55 (Eq. 5.6); S_u,ave = 0.6 ksf (top, desiccated surface soils excluded) and (1.50 + 2.07)/2 = 1.79 ksf (bottom, 2.07 interpolated at 58.5 ft); f_s = 0.33 and 0.98 ksf; R_S = 0.33 x pi x 1.5 x 24 + 0.98 x pi x 1.5 x 29.5 = 37.3 + 136.2 = 173.5 kips. End-bearing by Eqs. 5.4 and 5.7: S_u = (2.10 + 2.14)/2 = 2.12 ksf = 1.06 tsf (interpolated at 60 and 63 ft), N*_c = 8.71 from Table 5.1, q_p = 8.71 x 2.12 = 18.46 ksf, R_B = 18.46 x (pi/4) x 1.5^2 = 32.6 kips (p. 126).
